q: What percentage of vertebral compression fractures are actually symptomatic?
o: Approximately 93%
Approximately 30% to 40%
Approximately 52%
Approximately 21%
explanation:
Only approximately 30% to 40% of vertebral compression fractures are symptomatic (p1631).

A. Approximately 93%: 93% is degenerative disc disease in one asymptomatic over-60 imaging sample, not symptomatic compression fractures (p1636).
C. Approximately 52%: 52% is disc bulge in one asymptomatic MRI study, not symptomatic compression fractures (p1636).
D. Approximately 21%: 21% is spinal stenosis in an asymptomatic over-60 sample, not symptomatic compression fractures (p1636).

q: Roughly what proportion of patients who sustain one vertebral fracture will have another within 5 years?
o: Over 20%
Approximately 93%
Approximately 52%
Approximately 30% to 40%
explanation:
Studies suggest over 20% of patients sustaining a fracture have another fracture within five years (p1631).

D. Approximately 30% to 40%: This is the approximate fraction of vertebral compression fractures that are symptomatic (p1631).
B. Approximately 93%: This is degenerative disc disease prevalence in an asymptomatic over-60 imaging sample (p1636).
C. Approximately 52%: This is the SPORT nonoperative-to-surgery crossover fraction at eight years (p1639).

q: In older adults, what is a key pitfall in recognizing infectious back pain (eg, discitis/osteomyelitis)?
o: Endovascular infection risk excludes a spinal infectious cause
Disc infection cannot mimic mechanical disc disease
Fever can be absent despite spinal infection
Fever must accompany all infectious back pain
explanation:
Fever can be absent in older patients with spinal infection, so its absence does not exclude infection (p1631).

D. Fever must accompany all infectious back pain: The text explicitly allows absence of fever (p1631).
B. Disc infection cannot mimic mechanical disc disease: The signs and symptoms can mimic mechanical disc disease (p1631).
A. Endovascular infection risk excludes a spinal infectious cause: Such risk should heighten suspicion for an infectious cause (p1631).

q: How do you distinguish neurogenic claudication from vascular claudication on exercise testing?
o: Both conditions resolve on the treadmill because spinal extension increases canal diameter
Both conditions improve on the bicycle because spinal flexion reduces vascular symptoms
Neurogenic symptoms improve on the bicycle; vascular symptoms persist on both tests
Neurogenic symptoms persist on both tests; vascular symptoms improve on the bicycle
explanation:
Neurogenic claudication worsens on the treadmill and improves on a bicycle; vascular claudication persists with both tests (p1636).

D. Neurogenic symptoms persist on both tests; vascular symptoms improve on the bicycle: This reverses the stated distinction (p1636).
B. Both conditions improve on the bicycle because spinal flexion reduces vascular symptoms: Vascular claudication causes persistent difficulty on both tests (p1636).
A. Both conditions resolve on the treadmill because spinal extension increases canal diameter: Spinal flexion during cycling increases canal diameter; neurogenic symptoms worsen on the treadmill (p1636).

q: Why is lumbar spine imaging a poor stand-alone diagnostic tool in older adults?
o: A herniated nucleus pulposus always produces back symptoms
Lumbar imaging abnormalities are common in asymptomatic older adults
Any disc bulge on MRI necessarily explains the clinical pain
Disc degeneration is absent in asymptomatic people older than 60
explanation:
Anatomic lumbar abnormalities are common in asymptomatic older adults, so imaging alone cannot establish the cause of back pain (p1636).

D. Disc degeneration is absent in asymptomatic people older than 60: One asymptomatic study found degenerative disc disease in 93% of subjects over 60 (p1636).
C. Any disc bulge on MRI necessarily explains the clinical pain: Disc bulges occurred in asymptomatic subjects (p1636).
A. A herniated nucleus pulposus always produces back symptoms: One asymptomatic over-60 sample had a herniated nucleus pulposus in 36% (p1636).

q: In the epidural steroid injection RCT of 400 older adults with lumbar spinal stenosis, what did adding glucocorticoid to lidocaine achieve?
o: Proof that lidocaine alone has no effect compared with placebo
Minimal or no additional short-term disability or leg-pain benefit
Proof that steroid injections outperform a placebo injection
A clear additional short-term disability and leg-pain benefit
explanation:
The 400-patient trial found minimal or no additional short-term disability or leg-pain benefit from adding glucocorticoid to lidocaine; it had no placebo arm (p1639).

D. A clear additional short-term disability and leg-pain benefit: The reported comparison showed minimal or no short-term benefit (p1639).
C. Proof that steroid injections outperform a placebo injection: The trial included no placebo group (p1639).
A. Proof that lidocaine alone has no effect compared with placebo: Without a placebo arm, that comparison was not made (p1639).

q: In the SPORT trial, what fraction of the nonoperative arm had crossed over to surgery by 8 years?
explanation:
At eight-year SPORT follow-up, 52% of those randomized to nonoperative treatment had undergone surgery (p1639).

A. 36%: This is herniated nucleus pulposus prevalence in an asymptomatic over-60 MRI sample (p1636).
C. 21%: This is spinal stenosis prevalence in that asymptomatic sample (p1636).
D. 93%: This is degenerative disc disease prevalence in that sample (p1636).
